title: PyTorch Examples
description: Small PyTorch examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Create a tensor
examples.description: A PyTorch tensor stores numbers with a shape and a data type. torch.tensor makes one from a small Python list.

examples.title: Inspect shape and dimensions
examples.description: Shape gives the size of each dimension. ndim tells you how many dimensions there are.
examples.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(tuple(x.shape), x.ndim)

examples.title: Set a dtype
examples.description: A dtype specifies how numbers are represented. Floating-point tensors are commonly used for model calculations and gradients.
examples.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.float32)
print(x.dtype)

examples.title: Add matching values
examples.description: Tensor arithmetic can combine matching positions. Shapes must match or follow broadcasting rules.
examples.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([1, 2])
b = torch.tensor([3, 4])
print((a + b).tolist())

examples.title: Use matrix multiplication
examples.description: Matrix multiplication combines rows with columns. The inner dimensions must match. It is different from element-wise multiplication.
examples.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]])
b = torch.tensor([[3.], [4.]])
print((a @ b).item())

examples.title: Reshape values
examples.description: reshape changes the layout of a tensor while keeping the same number of values.

examples.title: Track a gradient
examples.description: requires_grad asks PyTorch to track operations for automatic differentiation. backward fills the gradient of the scalar result with respect to the input.
examples.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x * x
y.backward()
print(x.grad.item())

examples.title: Disable tracking for a calculation
examples.description: torch.no_grad runs operations without building a gradient-tracking graph. This is useful when you only need predictions.
examples.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    y = x * 2
print(y.requires_grad)

examples.title: A linear layer learns weights
examples.description: nn.Linear combines input features into output values using learned weights and a bias. Two inputs can produce one output.
examples.code:
import torch

layer = torch.nn.Linear(2, 1)
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])
print(tuple(layer(x).shape))

examples.title: Build a small sequential model
examples.description: A sequential model applies layers in order. An activation such as ReLU keeps positive values and changes negative values to zero.
examples.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 3), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(3, 1))
print(tuple(model(torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])).shape))

examples.title: One training step
examples.description: A training step clears old gradients, computes loss, finds new gradients and updates weights. Each step has a separate job.
examples.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
x = torch.tensor([[1.], [2.]])
y = torch.tensor([[2.], [4.]])
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x), y)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
print(loss.item() >= 0)

examples.title: Evaluation mode and checking
examples.description: model.eval switches training-sensitive layers to evaluation behaviour. Use it with no_grad when making ordinary evaluation predictions.
examples.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, 1))
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    result = model(torch.tensor([[3.0]]))
print(tuple(result.shape))
